lessons.title: Defining Health & Wellbeing + Physical Factors
lessons.description: What health and wellbeing really means, plus inherited conditions, physical and mental ill health.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Health and Wellbeing?

Many people think being “healthy” simply means not being ill. The Pearson BTEC specification uses a much broader definition. Health and wellbeing is a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing — it is not just the absence of disease or illness. This means a person can be physically fit but still have poor wellbeing if they feel lonely, stressed, or unhappy.

Key Fact

Health and wellbeing is defined as a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing, and not just the absence of disease or illness.

This definition matters because it shapes how health and social care professionals assess and support individuals. They do not just treat physical symptoms — they consider a person’s mental state, relationships, and overall quality of life. Throughout this unit, you will see factors that affect health and wellbeing grouped into physical, lifestyle, social, cultural, economic, and environmental categories.

Inherited Conditions

Some health conditions are passed from parents to children through inherited conditions. These are caused by faulty genes and are present from birth, though symptoms may not appear immediately. The specification requires you to know two key examples.

Sickle cell disease affects the red blood cells, which become crescent-shaped instead of round. This means they can block blood vessels and do not carry oxygen as effectively. Symptoms include episodes of severe pain (called crises), fatigue, and increased risk of infections. It affects physical wellbeing through pain and tiredness, emotional wellbeing through frustration and anxiety about crises, and social wellbeing because hospital stays and absences from school or work can lead to isolation.

Cystic fibrosis causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system. This leads to frequent chest infections, difficulty breathing, and problems absorbing nutrients from food. Daily physiotherapy and medication are needed. The condition affects all areas of PIES development — physically through breathing difficulties, intellectually through missed education, emotionally through frustration at limitations, and socially through feeling different from peers.

Physical Ill Health

Physical ill health covers conditions that damage the body’s normal functions. The specification names three conditions you must know.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a general term for conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, including coronary heart disease, heart attacks, and strokes. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, poor diet, and lack of exercise. CVD can limit a person’s physical abilities and create anxiety about future health events, reducing emotional wellbeing.

Obesity is when a person has an excessive amount of body fat, usually measured using BMI. A BMI of 30 or above is classified as obese. Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, joint problems, and some cancers. It can also affect emotional wellbeing through low self-esteem and social wellbeing through bullying or discrimination.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body does not produce enough insulin or the body’s cells do not react to insulin properly. This leads to high blood sugar levels. It is strongly linked to obesity, poor diet, and lack of physical activity. If unmanaged, it can cause serious complications including nerve damage, kidney problems, and vision loss.

Key Fact

CVD, obesity, and type 2 diabetes are closely linked — they share common risk factors such as poor diet, lack of physical activity, and smoking. Obesity significantly increases the risk of developing both CVD and type 2 diabetes.

Mental Ill Health

Mental ill health affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. The two conditions named in the specification are anxiety and stress.

Anxiety involves persistent feelings of worry, fear, or nervousness that are difficult to control. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, sweating, and difficulty sleeping. Anxiety can prevent a person from socialising, attending work or school, and enjoying daily activities — affecting all areas of their PIES development.

Stress is the body’s reaction to feeling threatened or under pressure. Short-term stress can be helpful (motivating someone before an exam), but long-term stress damages health. Chronic stress can cause headaches, high blood pressure, digestive problems, weakened immunity, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and withdrawal from relationships.

Physical Abilities and Sensory Impairments

Physical abilities refer to what a person can physically do — walking, lifting, gripping, and so on. Conditions like arthritis, cerebral palsy, or injuries from accidents can reduce physical abilities. This can affect independence, employment opportunities, and self-esteem.

Sensory impairments affect the senses, most commonly sight and hearing. A person who is deaf or blind faces challenges in communication, accessing information, and navigating their environment. Sensory impairments can lead to social isolation if support is not available, and may affect emotional wellbeing through frustration or dependency on others.

Both physical abilities and sensory impairments highlight why the definition of health and wellbeing goes beyond “absence of disease” — a person may have a stable condition but still experience reduced wellbeing if they lack support, face discrimination, or feel excluded from social activities.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Component 3 exam, questions often use a case study about a named individual. When explaining how a physical factor affects health and wellbeing, always link your answer to all relevant areas of PIES (Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, Social). For example, if asked about the impact of obesity, explain the physical effects (joint pain, increased disease risk), then show how these lead to emotional effects (low self-esteem) and social effects (bullying, isolation). The best answers make chains of reasoning — one effect leading to another.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health and wellbeing is a combination of physical health and social and emotional wellbeing — not just the absence of disease or illness.
  • Inherited conditions (sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis), physical ill health (CVD, obesity, type 2 diabetes), and mental ill health (anxiety, stress) all affect multiple areas of PIES development.
  • Physical abilities and sensory impairments can reduce independence and social participation, showing why wellbeing is about more than just physical health.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which inherited conditions have a greater impact on an individual's health and wellbeing than physical ill health conditions such as obesity or type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Inherited conditions:
• Present from birth — individual has no control
• Often lifelong with no cure (e.g. sickle cell, cystic fibrosis)
• Affect PIES from an early age — missed education, social isolation from childhood
• Daily treatment regimes can be exhausting and restrictive
Physical ill health:
• Often linked to lifestyle choices — some can be prevented or managed
• Obesity and type 2 diabetes can be improved with diet and exercise
• However, CVD can be fatal if not managed
• Social stigma around obesity can severely affect emotional wellbeing
Conclusion: Both have significant impacts but inherited conditions may be considered greater because the individual has no control and they are lifelong. However, the impact depends on the severity of the condition, the support available, and the individual's circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Amir is 45 years old. He was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. He works long hours in a stressful office job and rarely exercises. He has also been feeling anxious about his health. Using the case study, assess how Amir's physical factors are affecting his overall health and wellbeing. In your answer, consider the impact on his physical, intellectual, emotional, and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive, well-developed response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Amir's specific circumstances. Chains of reasoning throughout.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some developed links to the case study.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development or links to Amir.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure increase risk of CVD, stroke, kidney damage. Lack of exercise worsens both conditions. Fatigue and physical symptoms reduce his ability to function.
• Intellectual: Stress and anxiety can cause difficulty concentrating at work. High blood sugar levels can cause brain fog. This may affect his job performance.
• Emotional: Anxiety about his health creates persistent worry. He may feel guilty about his lifestyle. Low mood and fear about long-term complications. Stress from work compounds his emotional state.
• Social: Long working hours reduce time for socialising. Anxiety may cause him to withdraw from friends and family. He may avoid social events involving food or alcohol due to his diabetes.
• Links between factors: stress (mental ill health) raises blood pressure (physical ill health), creating a negative cycle. Lack of exercise worsens both diabetes and anxiety.
• Person-specific: At 45, Amir is in middle adulthood where health risks increase naturally. His stressful job is both a cause and an aggravating factor.

lessons.title: Lifestyle Factors Affecting Health
lessons.description: How nutrition, exercise, smoking, and substance misuse affect health and wellbeing.
lessons.content_html:
Why Lifestyle Factors Matter

Unlike inherited conditions, lifestyle factors are things people can control. The choices a person makes about what they eat, how active they are, and whether they smoke or misuse substances directly affect their health and wellbeing. The Component 3 specification identifies four key lifestyle factors: nutrition, physical activity, smoking, and substance misuse.

Each lifestyle factor can have both positive and negative effects on health and wellbeing. A balanced diet supports good physical health, while a poor diet increases the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The exam will often ask you to explain how a specific lifestyle factor affects an individual across the PIES categories.

Nutrition

Nutrition refers to the food and drink a person consumes and how the body uses it. A balanced diet provides the right amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water. Good nutrition supports physical growth, brain function, emotional stability, and the energy needed to socialise and participate in activities.

Key Fact

A balanced diet positively affects all areas of PIES: physical (healthy weight, energy, strong immune system), intellectual (brain function, concentration), emotional (stable mood, positive self-image), social (energy to socialise, shared meals with others).

Poor nutrition includes both malnutrition (not getting enough nutrients) and over-nutrition (eating too much of the wrong foods). Malnutrition can weaken the immune system, slow growth in young people, and cause tiredness. Over-nutrition leads to obesity, which increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, and joint problems. Both affect emotional wellbeing through low energy and poor self-image, and social wellbeing through reduced ability to participate in activities.

Physical Activity

Regular physical activity is essential for maintaining good health. The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, while children and young people should aim for 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.

The benefits of regular physical activity span all areas of PIES. Physically, it strengthens the heart, muscles, and bones, helps maintain a healthy weight, and reduces the risk of CVD, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. Intellectually, exercise improves concentration, memory, and cognitive function by increasing blood flow to the brain. Emotionally, physical activity releases endorphins (natural mood-boosting chemicals), reduces stress and anxiety, and improves self-esteem. Socially, team sports and group exercise classes provide opportunities to meet people and build friendships.

A lack of physical activity (a sedentary lifestyle) has the opposite effect. It increases the risk of obesity, weakens muscles and bones, reduces concentration, worsens mood, and limits social opportunities. Prolonged inactivity is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety.

Smoking

Smoking tobacco is one of the biggest preventable causes of ill health in the UK. Cigarettes contain nicotine (which is highly addictive), tar (which damages the lungs), and carbon monoxide (which reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry).

Physical: Smoking causes lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), heart disease, and strokes. It reduces lung capacity, causes breathlessness, and ages the skin prematurely. Intellectual: Reduced oxygen supply to the brain can impair concentration and memory. Emotional: While smokers often say smoking reduces stress, the addiction cycle actually increases anxiety between cigarettes. Worrying about health consequences adds further stress. Social: Smoking can cause social exclusion as non-smokers may avoid being around smoke. The cost of cigarettes reduces money available for social activities. Smoking bans in public places limit where smokers can go.

Key Fact

Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the UK. It damages the lungs, heart, and blood vessels, and the nicotine in tobacco creates a powerful addiction that makes quitting extremely difficult.

Substance Misuse

Substance misuse means using substances in a way that is harmful to health. The specification names three substances: alcohol, cannabis, and opiates (e.g. heroin).

Alcohol: Excessive drinking damages the liver (leading to cirrhosis), increases the risk of heart disease and some cancers, impairs judgement and coordination, and can lead to addiction (alcoholism). It affects emotional wellbeing through mood swings and depression, and social wellbeing through damaged relationships, aggression, and financial problems. The UK CMO guidelines recommend no more than 14 units per week for both men and women.

Cannabis: This is an illegal drug that can be smoked or eaten. It affects concentration, memory, and motivation. Long-term use is linked to mental health problems including anxiety, paranoia, and psychosis. It can also damage the lungs when smoked. Socially, cannabis use can lead to legal problems, reduced employment prospects, and damaged relationships.

Opiates (e.g. heroin): Opiates are highly addictive drugs that depress the central nervous system. Heroin use carries risks of overdose (which can be fatal), infections from sharing needles (including HIV and hepatitis), collapsed veins, and severe constipation. Addiction dominates the user’s life, leading to loss of employment, breakdown of relationships, criminal behaviour to fund the habit, and homelessness. Opiates have devastating effects across all areas of PIES.

Substance misuse does not just affect the individual — it impacts families, friendships, and communities. Children growing up with a parent who misuses substances may experience neglect, emotional trauma, and instability. The financial cost of addiction can push families into poverty.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about lifestyle factors, always use the PIES framework to structure your answer. State the factor, explain the effect on a specific PIES area, then develop the point by showing the consequence. For case study questions, link every point back to the named individual — generic answers that do not reference the case study will not reach the highest mark bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lifestyle factors (nutrition, physical activity, smoking, substance misuse) are choices that can positively or negatively affect health and wellbeing across all PIES areas.
  • Good nutrition and regular physical activity support physical health, brain function, emotional stability, and social participation.
  • Smoking and substance misuse (alcohol, cannabis, opiates) create addiction, damage physical health, and have devastating effects on emotional and social wellbeing.

practice_questions.text: Priya is 17 years old. She has started drinking alcohol at weekends with friends and has recently tried cannabis. She has been skipping meals and her school attendance has dropped. Her parents are worried about her behaviour. Using the case study, assess how Priya's lifestyle factors are affecting her overall health and wellbeing. Consider the impact on her physical, intellectual, emotional, and social development.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Priya's specific circumstances and chains of reasoning.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some links to the case study.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Alcohol damages the liver and brain (still developing at 17). Skipping meals leads to malnutrition — weakened immune system, lack of energy. Cannabis damages lungs.
• Intellectual: Cannabis impairs concentration and memory. Skipping meals reduces brain function. Dropped school attendance means missed learning — affects academic achievement.
• Emotional: Alcohol is a depressant — may worsen mood. Cannabis linked to anxiety and paranoia. Conflict with parents causes stress. May feel guilt or worry about her behaviour.
• Social: Drinking with friends may seem positive socially, but risky behaviour can damage friendships. Conflict with parents strains family relationships. Dropped attendance reduces school friendships.
• Links: At 17, Priya is in adolescence where peer pressure is strong and brain development is ongoing — substance misuse at this age can have long-lasting effects. The combination of multiple negative lifestyle factors compounds the impact.
• Synoptic links: Parents' concern shows impact on family relationships (Component 1). Support services could help (Component 2).

lessons.title: Social, Cultural & Economic Factors
lessons.description: How relationships, culture, discrimination, employment, and finances affect wellbeing.
lessons.content_html:
Social Factors

The people around us have a powerful influence on our health and wellbeing. Social factors include the quality of relationships, whether a person feels included or excluded, and whether they experience bullying or discrimination. These factors can have positive or negative effects across all areas of PIES.

Supportive and Unsupportive Relationships

Supportive relationships with friends, family, peers, and colleagues provide encouragement, practical help, and a sense of belonging. A person who feels supported is more likely to have high self-esteem, manage stress effectively, and maintain good mental health. Family support can encourage healthy eating and exercise, while supportive friendships provide emotional comfort and social opportunities.

Unsupportive relationships have the opposite effect. If a person’s family is critical, neglectful, or abusive, it can lead to low self-esteem, anxiety, depression, and social withdrawal. Unsupportive relationships at work can cause chronic stress, reduced motivation, and difficulty concentrating. Children who grow up without stable, loving relationships may struggle with emotional regulation and forming healthy relationships later in life.

Key Fact

Supportive relationships positively affect all PIES areas: physical (encouragement to stay healthy), intellectual (motivation to learn), emotional (security, self-esteem), social (sense of belonging). Unsupportive relationships have the opposite effect across all areas.

Social Inclusion and Exclusion

Social inclusion means being part of a group or community — feeling accepted and valued. It supports emotional wellbeing by giving a sense of purpose and belonging. Social exclusion means being left out. It can happen because of poverty, disability, language barriers, age, or other factors. Excluded individuals may experience loneliness, depression, and reduced access to services, education, or employment opportunities.

Bullying and Discrimination

Bullying is repeated behaviour intended to hurt, intimidate, or control another person. It can be physical (hitting, pushing), verbal (name-calling, threats), or cyber (online harassment). Bullying severely damages emotional wellbeing, causing anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and in extreme cases, self-harm. It affects intellectual development through reduced concentration and school avoidance, and social development through isolation and fear of others.

Discrimination means treating someone unfairly because of a characteristic such as age, disability, race, gender, religion, or sexual orientation. It is protected against by the Equality Act 2010. Discrimination in the workplace can limit career progression and income. In healthcare, it can prevent people from accessing the services they need. Experiencing discrimination damages self-esteem, creates stress, and can lead to social withdrawal and poorer health outcomes.

Cultural Factors

Cultural factors relate to the beliefs, values, and practices of the communities people belong to. They shape behaviours and attitudes that can positively or negatively affect health and wellbeing.

Religion: Religious belief can provide a strong sense of community, moral guidance, and emotional support through prayer, worship, and fellowship. However, some religious practices may restrict access to certain medical treatments (e.g. blood transfusions) or create conflict if an individual’s beliefs differ from their family or community.

Gender roles and expectations: Traditional gender roles may limit opportunities — for example, expecting women to be primary carers can restrict career progression and financial independence. Pressure on men to be “strong” and not show emotion can prevent them from seeking help for mental health problems.

Gender identity: An individual whose gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth may face discrimination, bullying, or rejection from family and peers. This can severely affect emotional wellbeing and mental health. Acceptance and support have the opposite, positive effect.

Sexual orientation: Individuals who identify as LGBTQ+ may experience discrimination, prejudice, or bullying, which negatively affects emotional and social wellbeing. In supportive environments, being able to express one’s identity freely has a positive effect on self-esteem and social inclusion.

Community participation: Being involved in community activities (volunteering, clubs, religious groups, sports teams) provides social connections, a sense of purpose, and opportunities for physical activity. It can improve all areas of PIES. Lack of community participation can lead to isolation and loneliness.

Economic Factors

Economic factors relate to money, employment, and financial resources. They have a significant impact on an individual’s ability to access the things needed for good health and wellbeing.

Employment situation: Having a job provides income, routine, social interaction, and a sense of purpose. These positively affect all PIES areas. Unemployment can lead to financial hardship, loss of routine, reduced social contact, low self-esteem, stress, and depression. Long-term unemployment is strongly linked to poor mental and physical health.

Financial resources: These include income (from employment), inheritance, and savings. Having adequate financial resources allows a person to afford nutritious food, suitable housing, heating, healthcare, and leisure activities. Poverty restricts access to all of these, increasing the risk of poor diet, cold or damp housing, stress, and social exclusion. Research consistently shows that people living in poverty have poorer health outcomes and shorter life expectancy than those who are financially secure.

Key Fact

Economic factors underpin many other factors. Poverty can lead to poor nutrition, inadequate housing, limited access to healthcare, and chronic stress — affecting all areas of PIES development.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For higher-mark questions on social, cultural, and economic factors, show how factors link together. For example, discrimination (social) may lead to unemployment (economic), which causes poverty (economic), leading to poor housing (environmental) and poor diet (lifestyle). The best answers create chains of cause and effect rather than listing isolated points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Social factors (relationships, inclusion/exclusion, bullying, discrimination) directly affect emotional and social wellbeing but also impact physical and intellectual health.
  • Cultural factors (religion, gender roles, gender identity, sexual orientation, community participation) shape behaviours and experiences that can support or hinder wellbeing.
  • Economic factors (employment, income, savings) underpin many other factors — poverty restricts access to nutrition, housing, healthcare, and social opportunities.

lessons.title: Environmental Factors & Life Events
lessons.description: How housing, pollution, and major life events affect physical and emotional wellbeing.
lessons.content_html:
Environmental Factors

The environment in which a person lives, works, and spends their time has a direct effect on their health and wellbeing. Environmental factors include housing conditions, the home environment, and exposure to different types of pollution. Unlike lifestyle factors, individuals may have limited control over their environment — especially if they are affected by poverty or live in a deprived area.

Housing

The specification identifies three aspects of housing: housing needs, housing conditions, and housing location.

Housing needs relate to whether a home is suitable for the people living in it. An elderly person needs a home without stairs or with a stairlift. A family with young children needs enough bedrooms and a safe outdoor space. Overcrowding occurs when there are too many people for the size of the property, leading to stress, lack of privacy, poor sleep, and increased spread of infections.

Housing conditions refer to the state of the property itself. Damp, cold, and poorly maintained homes increase the risk of respiratory conditions like asthma, cause joint pain, and create an unpleasant living environment. Mould growth in damp homes can trigger allergies and breathing problems. Poor housing conditions are strongly linked to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem because the individual feels they have no control over their living situation.

Key Fact

Poor housing conditions (damp, cold, overcrowding) negatively affect physical health (respiratory problems, infections), emotional wellbeing (stress, anxiety, low self-esteem), and social wellbeing (embarrassment about inviting people home, lack of private space).

Housing location affects access to services, employment, education, and social opportunities. Living in a rural area may mean long distances to hospitals, shops, and schools, leading to social isolation. Living in an area with high crime rates can cause fear and anxiety. Conversely, living in a safe neighbourhood with good transport links, parks, and community facilities supports positive health and wellbeing.

Home Environment

The home environment refers to the atmosphere within the home — not just the physical building but the relationships, routines, and emotional climate. A warm, clean, safe, and loving home environment supports positive development across all PIES areas. A chaotic, dirty, unsafe, or hostile home environment has the opposite effect.

For example, a child growing up in a home where there is domestic violence will experience fear, anxiety, and insecurity (emotional), difficulty concentrating at school (intellectual), potential physical harm (physical), and difficulty forming healthy relationships (social). The home environment is particularly important for children and young people, as it shapes their development during critical life stages.

Exposure to Pollution

The specification identifies three types of pollution that affect health and wellbeing.

Air pollution: Caused by traffic fumes, industrial emissions, and burning fossil fuels. It worsens respiratory conditions like asthma and COPD, increases the risk of lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, and can cause headaches and fatigue. People living near busy roads or in cities are most affected.

Noise pollution: Caused by traffic, construction, aircraft, and loud neighbours. Prolonged exposure to noise can cause hearing damage, sleep disturbance, increased stress and anxiety, difficulty concentrating, raised blood pressure, and irritability. It particularly affects emotional and intellectual wellbeing.

Light pollution: Caused by excessive artificial lighting from street lights, buildings, and screens. It disrupts sleep patterns by interfering with the body’s natural circadian rhythm (sleep-wake cycle). Poor sleep leads to fatigue, reduced concentration, weakened immunity, and increased stress. Screen use before bed is a common cause of light pollution affecting young people.

Life Events

A life event is a significant event or change that affects a person’s development. Life events can be expected (planned, like retirement) or unexpected (unplanned, like an accident). The specification groups life events into three categories and requires you to understand how they impact PIES development.

Key Fact

Life events are grouped into three categories: physical events (accident/injury, physical illness, mental and emotional health), relationship changes (marriage, divorce, parenthood, bereavement), and life circumstances (moving house/school/job, redundancy, imprisonment, retirement).

Physical Events

Accident or injury can cause pain, disability, and loss of independence (physical), difficulty concentrating or returning to work or education (intellectual), fear, frustration, and anxiety about recovery (emotional), and social isolation if mobility is reduced (social). Physical illness has similar effects — a serious diagnosis like cancer affects every area of PIES. Mental and emotional health events such as developing depression or experiencing a breakdown affect the ability to function in daily life, maintain relationships, and engage with education or work.

Relationship Changes

Marriage or civil partnership can positively affect wellbeing by providing emotional security, companionship, and shared financial resources. However, it can also bring stress if the relationship is difficult. Divorce or separation can cause grief, loss of income, disruption to children’s lives, loss of shared friendships, and reduced self-esteem. Parenthood brings joy and purpose but also exhaustion, financial pressure, and reduced social life. Bereavement — the death of a loved one — causes grief, loneliness, and can trigger depression. It affects all PIES areas and the impact can last months or years.

Moving house, school, or job can be exciting but also stressful — it disrupts routines, removes familiar social networks, and requires adaptation to new environments. Children who move schools frequently may struggle academically and socially. Exclusion from education removes access to learning, peer relationships, and routine. Redundancy causes loss of income, purpose, and social contact. Imprisonment separates the individual from family and community, causes stigma, and limits future employment. Retirement provides freedom from work pressure but can lead to loss of purpose, reduced social contact, and financial anxiety if income drops.

The impact of any life event depends on the individual’s resilience, the support available to them, and their personal circumstances. Two people experiencing the same life event may respond very differently.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When discussing life events in the exam, always consider the individual’s life stage (Component 1). A bereavement affects a child differently from an adult. Redundancy impacts someone in early adulthood (career-building stage) differently from someone in later adulthood (near retirement). Making these synoptic links to other components earns higher marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Environmental factors (housing needs/conditions/location, home environment, air/noise/light pollution) directly affect physical health and emotional wellbeing, often beyond the individual’s control.
  • Life events fall into three categories: physical events, relationship changes, and life circumstances — each can have positive and negative effects across PIES.
  • The impact of life events depends on the individual’s resilience, available support, and personal circumstances.

• Social: Living alone with family far away limits social contact. Third floor with no lift may prevent her from going out to socialise. Loneliness is a major risk factor for poor health in later adulthood.

• Synoptic: In later adulthood, physical decline is expected (Component 1). Health and social care services could provide support (Component 2) — housing adaptations, bereavement counselling, social groups.

lessons.title: Physiological Health Indicators
lessons.description: Interpreting resting heart rate, blood pressure, BMI, and the risks of abnormal readings.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Physiological Indicators?

Physiological indicators are measurable physical signs that health professionals use to assess a person’s current state of health. They provide objective data — actual numbers that can be compared against published guidelines to determine whether someone is healthy or at risk. The Component 3 specification requires you to know four key indicators: resting heart rate, heart rate recovery after exercise, blood pressure, and body mass index (BMI).

Understanding these indicators is important because they allow health professionals to identify health risks early, before symptoms develop. Abnormal readings can be a warning sign of underlying conditions that need attention.

Resting Heart Rate

Resting heart rate (also called resting pulse) measures how many times the heart beats per minute when the body is completely at rest. The normal range is 60 to 100 bpm (beats per minute).

Key Fact

Normal resting heart rate: 60 to 100 bpm. A lower resting heart rate generally indicates better cardiovascular fitness, as the heart pumps more blood per beat. Athletes may have resting rates below 60 bpm.

A resting heart rate that is consistently above 100 bpm (tachycardia) may indicate stress, anxiety, dehydration, anaemia, thyroid problems, or heart conditions. It means the heart is working harder than it should, which over time can increase the risk of heart failure. A rate consistently below 60 bpm (bradycardia) in a non-athlete may indicate problems with the heart’s electrical system and can cause dizziness, fatigue, and fainting.

Heart Rate Recovery After Exercise

Heart rate recovery measures how quickly the heart returns to its resting rate after physical activity. The faster the recovery, the fitter the individual. A healthy person’s heart rate should drop significantly within the first minute after stopping exercise — typically by at least 15 to 25 bpm.

Slow heart rate recovery is a sign of poor cardiovascular fitness and may indicate an increased risk of heart disease. If someone’s heart takes several minutes to return to normal, it suggests the heart and circulatory system are not functioning efficiently. This indicator is useful because it shows how well the body copes under stress — not just at rest.

Blood Pressure

Blood pressure measures the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. It is recorded as two numbers: systolic (pressure when the heart beats) over diastolic (pressure when the heart rests between beats), measured in mmHg.

Low blood pressure: 90/60 mmHg or lower. Can cause dizziness, fainting, and fatigue. May indicate dehydration, blood loss, or an underlying medical condition.

Ideal blood pressure: Between 90/60 mmHg and 120/80 mmHg. The heart and blood vessels are functioning well.

Pre-high blood pressure: Between 120/80 mmHg and 140/90 mmHg. A warning sign that lifestyle changes are needed to prevent progression to high blood pressure.

High blood pressure (hypertension): 140/90 mmHg or higher. Often called the “silent killer” because it usually has no symptoms but significantly increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney disease.

High blood pressure is particularly dangerous because most people do not know they have it. Risk factors include obesity, high salt intake, lack of exercise, stress, smoking, and excessive alcohol consumption. It can be managed through lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, reducing salt) and medication.

Body Mass Index (BMI)

BMI is a calculation used to estimate whether a person is a healthy weight for their height. It is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared: \(\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}\).

Underweight: Below 18.5 kg/m². May indicate malnutrition, eating disorders, or underlying illness. Risks include weakened immune system, osteoporosis, and fertility problems.

Healthy weight: Between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m². Lower risk of weight-related health problems.

Overweight: Between 25 and 29.9 kg/m². Increased risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, and joint problems.

Obese: Between 30 and 39.9 kg/m². Significantly increased risk of serious health conditions.

Severely obese: 40 kg/m² or above. Very high risk of life-threatening conditions including heart disease, stroke, and some cancers.

BMI has limitations. It does not distinguish between muscle and fat — a muscular athlete may have a high BMI but be very healthy. It also does not show where fat is stored (abdominal fat is more dangerous than fat on the hips). Despite these limitations, BMI remains a widely used screening tool because it is quick, cheap, and provides a useful starting point for health assessments.

Significance of Abnormal Readings

The specification requires you to understand the significance of abnormal physiological readings in terms of both short-term risks (impact on current physical health) and long-term risks (potential future health problems).

Key Fact

Short-term risks of abnormal readings include dizziness, fatigue, breathlessness, and fainting. Long-term risks include heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, and reduced life expectancy.

For example, high blood pressure in the short term may cause no noticeable symptoms (hence “silent killer”), but in the long term it significantly increases the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, and vision problems. A high BMI in the short term may cause breathlessness and joint pain, while in the long term it increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, and some cancers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The exam may give you actual physiological data for a case study individual and ask you to interpret it. Always compare the reading to the published guideline range, state whether it is normal/low/high, and then explain the short-term and long-term risks. For example: “A blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg is above the high blood pressure threshold of 140/90 mmHg. In the short term, this may cause no symptoms, but in the long term it increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four physiological indicators: resting heart rate (60–100 bpm), heart rate recovery after exercise, blood pressure (ideal 90/60 to 120/80 mmHg), and BMI (healthy 18.5–24.9 kg/m²).
  • Abnormal readings carry both short-term risks (current symptoms like dizziness, fatigue) and long-term risks (future conditions like heart attack, stroke, diabetes).
  • Physiological indicators provide objective, measurable data that help health professionals identify health risks early and recommend appropriate actions.

• Long term: high blood pressure significantly increases the risk of heart attack and stroke (1) because the constant pressure damages the walls of the arteries, causing them to narrow and harden over time (1).
• Accept kidney disease, vision problems as alternative long-term risks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the usefulness of BMI as a physiological indicator of health.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Balanced discussion of both advantages and limitations.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points.
Indicative content:
Advantages:
• Quick, cheap, and easy to calculate
• Provides a useful starting point for health assessments
• Widely used and understood by health professionals
• Categories (underweight to severely obese) give clear thresholds for action
Limitations:
• Does not distinguish between muscle and fat — athletes may show as 'overweight'
• Does not show where fat is stored — abdominal fat is more dangerous
• Does not account for age, gender, or ethnicity differences
• Can give a misleading picture for pregnant women or the elderly.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which physiological indicators alone can provide a complete picture of an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
What physiological indicators CAN tell us:
• Objective, measurable data about physical health
• Can identify hidden risks (e.g. high blood pressure with no symptoms)
• Provide benchmarks to track improvement over time
• Help health professionals make evidence-based recommendations
What they CANNOT tell us:
• Nothing about emotional wellbeing — a person with perfect readings may be depressed
• Nothing about social wellbeing — does not measure loneliness or relationships
• BMI has limitations (muscle vs fat, fat distribution)
• A single reading is a snapshot — does not show trends
• Lifestyle indicators also needed for a fuller picture
Conclusion: Physiological indicators are an essential starting point but cannot provide a complete picture alone. Health and wellbeing includes emotional and social dimensions that cannot be measured by physical tests. A person-centred approach uses physiological data alongside lifestyle indicators and personal circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Mark is 55 years old. His health check results show: resting heart rate 105 bpm, blood pressure 155/95 mmHg, BMI 32. He works a desk job and drives everywhere. Using the case study, assess what Mark's physiological indicators tell us about his current health and the risks he faces.

Upper-mid band (5-7): Good interpretation of indicators with some risk analysis.

Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to guidelines.

• Resting heart rate 105 bpm: Above normal range (60–100 bpm). Indicates his heart is working harder than it should. Short-term: may feel palpitations, breathlessness. Long-term: increased risk of heart failure. Linked to his sedentary desk job and lack of exercise.

• BMI 32: Obese (above 30 threshold). Short-term: breathlessness, joint pain, fatigue. Long-term: increased risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, some cancers.

lessons.title: Lifestyle Indicators & Guidelines
lessons.description: The Eatwell Guide, CMO guidelines for activity, smoking, alcohol, and substance misuse.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Lifestyle Indicators?

While physiological indicators measure physical data like heart rate and blood pressure, lifestyle indicators focus on what a person does — their daily choices and behaviours. Health professionals use published guidelines to compare an individual’s lifestyle against recommended standards. The Component 3 specification requires you to know five areas of lifestyle indicators and their associated guidelines.

Lifestyle indicators are important because they reveal the causes behind abnormal physiological readings. If someone has high blood pressure and a high BMI, lifestyle indicators help identify why — perhaps they eat too much salt, do not exercise, and drink excessively. This makes it possible to recommend specific, targeted actions for improvement.

Nutrition — The Eatwell Guide

The Eatwell Guide is the UK government’s visual guide to a healthy, balanced diet. It divides food into five groups and shows the proportions in which they should be eaten.

Fruit and vegetables: Should make up just over a third of the diet. At least 5 portions a day. Provide vitamins, minerals, and fibre.

Starchy carbohydrates: Should make up just over a third of the diet. Includes bread, rice, pasta, and potatoes. Choose wholegrain varieties where possible for more fibre.

Proteins: Includes beans, pulses, fish, eggs, and meat. Aim for two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily (e.g. salmon, mackerel). Choose lean cuts of meat and eat less processed meat.

Dairy and alternatives: Includes milk, cheese, and yoghurt. Choose lower-fat and lower-sugar options. Provides calcium for strong bones.

Oils and spreads: Needed in small amounts. Choose unsaturated oils (e.g. olive oil, rapeseed oil) rather than saturated fats (e.g. butter, lard).

Key Fact

The Eatwell Guide recommends: at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables per day, plenty of starchy carbohydrates (preferably wholegrain), some protein and dairy, and small amounts of unsaturated oils. It also advises drinking 6 to 8 glasses of fluid per day and limiting foods high in fat, salt, and sugar.

A health professional would compare an individual’s actual diet against the Eatwell Guide to identify areas for improvement. If someone eats very few vegetables, consumes too many sugary drinks, and regularly eats processed foods high in salt, these lifestyle choices increase their risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, CVD, and nutrient deficiencies.

Physical Activity — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK Chief Medical Officers’ (CMO) Physical Activity Guidelines set out the recommended levels of exercise for different age groups.

Children and young people (5–18 years): At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity every day, including activities that strengthen muscles and bones at least 3 days per week. They should also minimise the amount of time spent being sedentary (sitting for extended periods).

Adults (19–64 years): At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity (e.g. running, swimming). Additionally, adults should do strength-building activities on at least 2 days per week and reduce extended sitting time.

Older adults (65+ years): Same targets as adults, with added emphasis on activities that improve balance and coordination to reduce the risk of falls.

If an individual is not meeting these guidelines, they are at increased risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, depression, and some cancers. A health professional would assess the person’s current activity levels and recommend realistic ways to increase them.

Smoking — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK CMO’s position on smoking is clear: there is no safe level of smoking. The guidelines recommend complete abstinence — not smoking at all is the only way to avoid the health risks. Even light or occasional smoking increases the risk of lung cancer, heart disease, stroke, and COPD.

Key Fact

The CMO guideline for smoking is that there is no safe level. The only recommendation is to not smoke. For those who currently smoke, the recommendation is to quit completely using available support services such as NHS Smokefree.

Health professionals assess whether an individual smokes, how many cigarettes per day, and for how long. This data helps calculate the level of risk and the urgency of quitting. Support options include nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), prescription medications, counselling, and the NHS Smokefree helpline.

Alcohol — UK CMO Guidelines

The UK CMO Alcohol Guidelines recommend that both men and women should drink no more than 14 units of alcohol per week. These units should be spread over at least 3 days, with several alcohol-free days each week. There is no “safe” level of drinking, but staying within 14 units keeps the health risks low.

One unit of alcohol equals 10ml of pure alcohol. Examples: a single pub measure of spirits (25ml at 40%) = 1 unit; a small glass of wine (125ml at 12%) = 1.5 units; a pint of lower-strength beer (3.6%) = 2 units; a pint of higher-strength beer (5.2%) = 3 units. Many people underestimate how many units they consume because drink sizes and strengths vary. Binge drinking (consuming a large amount in a single session) is particularly harmful, even if the weekly total stays under 14 units.

Exceeding the alcohol guidelines increases the risk of liver disease, heart disease, stroke, some cancers (particularly mouth, throat, and liver), and mental health problems including depression and anxiety. A health professional would assess an individual’s weekly alcohol consumption and compare it against the 14-unit guideline to determine risk level.

Substance Misuse

For substance misuse, there are no “safe level” guidelines because the use of illegal substances like cannabis and opiates carries inherent health and legal risks. Health professionals assess whether an individual uses any substances, the type and frequency of use, and whether there are signs of dependency or addiction.

Key indicators of substance misuse problems include: using substances more frequently or in larger amounts over time, being unable to stop despite wanting to, neglecting responsibilities (work, family, education), needing more of the substance to achieve the same effect (tolerance), and experiencing withdrawal symptoms when not using. If substance misuse is identified, the individual may be referred to specialist services including drug and alcohol support teams, counselling, and rehabilitation programmes.

Lifestyle indicators work alongside physiological indicators to build a complete picture of a person’s health. For example, if an individual has high blood pressure (physiological) and the lifestyle assessment reveals they eat a high-salt diet, drink 25 units of alcohol per week, and do no exercise (lifestyle), the health professional can recommend specific, targeted changes — reduce salt, cut alcohol to 14 units, start gentle exercise. This is far more useful than simply telling the person their blood pressure is too high.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be given lifestyle data for a case study individual (e.g. “drinks 20 units of alcohol per week”, “exercises once a month”, “smokes 10 cigarettes per day”). Always compare the data against the published guideline and state whether the individual is meeting or exceeding the recommended levels. Then explain the health risks and suggest specific improvements. Using the correct guideline figures (14 units, 150 minutes, no safe level of smoking) shows the examiner you know the specification content.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lifestyle indicators assess an individual’s daily choices (diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol, substance use) against published guidelines to identify health risks.
  • Key guidelines: Eatwell Guide (balanced diet, 5 portions fruit and veg), CMO Physical Activity (150 min/week for adults, 60 min/day for young people), no safe level of smoking, and no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.
  • Lifestyle and physiological indicators work together — lifestyle data reveals the causes behind abnormal physiological readings, enabling targeted recommendations.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which the Eatwell Guide is useful for improving an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:
Strengths of the Eatwell Guide:
• Visual and easy to understand — shows proportions clearly
• Government-backed, evidence-based advice
• Covers all food groups so provides comprehensive guidance
• Recommends specific targets (5 portions fruit/veg, 6-8 glasses fluid)
• Useful benchmark for health professionals to assess diet
Limitations:
• Does not account for individual needs (e.g. allergies, cultural/religious dietary requirements)
• Does not consider portion sizes or calorie needs for different people
• Some people cannot afford to follow it — fresh fruit/veg can be expensive
• Knowing the guidelines does not mean people will follow them
• Does not address eating disorders or emotional relationship with food
Conclusion: The Eatwell Guide is a useful starting point for nutrition advice, but it needs to be adapted to individual circumstances using a person-centred approach. It works best when combined with personalised support and when barriers such as cost, access, and knowledge are addressed.

practice_questions.text: Darren is 42 years old. A lifestyle assessment reveals that he eats takeaways 5 nights a week and rarely eats fruit or vegetables. He does no exercise and drives to work. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and drinks around 25 units of alcohol per week. His physiological indicators show a BMI of 34 and blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg. Using the case study, assess how Darren's lifestyle indicators compare to published guidelines and explain the risks to his health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response comparing each lifestyle indicator against guidelines, identifying specific risks, and linking lifestyle to physiological data.

Indicative content:
• Nutrition: Eating takeaways 5 nights a week and rarely eating fruit/veg is far below the Eatwell Guide recommendation of 5 portions a day and a balanced diet. High salt, fat, and sugar intake increases risk of obesity (his BMI is already 34 — obese), CVD, and type 2 diabetes.
• Physical activity: No exercise and driving to work means he is well below the CMO guideline of 150 minutes moderate activity per week. Sedentary lifestyle contributes to his obesity and high blood pressure. Lack of exercise also affects mental health — no endorphin release.
• Smoking: 15 cigarettes a day — CMO guidelines state there is no safe level of smoking. He is at increased risk of lung cancer, COPD, heart disease, and stroke. Smoking also raises blood pressure (his is already 150/95).
• Alcohol: 25 units per week is nearly double the CMO guideline of 14 units. Increases risk of liver disease, heart disease, cancers, and depression. Combined with smoking and poor diet, the risks are compounded.
• Links to physiological data: His BMI of 34 (obese) and blood pressure of 150/95 (high) are directly linked to his poor lifestyle choices. If he follows the guidelines, both could improve significantly.
• Overall: Darren is exceeding or failing to meet every guideline. The combination of multiple unhealthy lifestyle factors creates a compound effect, significantly increasing his short-term and long-term health risks. A person-centred approach would prioritise the most urgent changes while considering his preferences and circumstances.

lessons.title: The Person-Centred Approach
lessons.description: How person-centred care considers needs, wishes and circumstances to benefit everyone.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the Person-Centred Approach?

The person-centred approach is a way of planning and delivering care that puts the individual at the heart of every decision. Instead of offering the same advice to everyone, health and social care professionals tailor their recommendations so they are realistic and meaningful for each person.

This approach links directly to the skills, attributes and values you studied in Component 2. It turns those values — such as empathy, communication and respect — into everyday practice.

Key Fact

A person-centred approach takes into account three things: the individual’s needs (to reduce health risks), their wishes (preferences and choices) and their circumstances (age, ability, location, living conditions, support available, and physical and emotional health).

Taking Account of Needs, Wishes & Circumstances

Needs are the health risks that must be addressed. For example, a person with high blood pressure needs recommendations that will lower it, such as reducing salt intake or increasing physical activity. The professional identifies the clinical priorities.

Wishes are the individual’s own preferences. A person who hates running should not be told to jog every day — they might prefer swimming or cycling. Ignoring wishes makes it far less likely that someone will follow the plan.

Circumstances cover everything about the individual’s situation. A single parent working shifts has less free time than a retired person. Someone living in a rural area may not have a gym nearby. A teenager with anxiety may need a different style of support from an older adult. Circumstances include age, ability, location, living conditions, existing support networks, and current physical and emotional health.

Jamil is 52 and has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He also has mobility problems due to arthritis in his knees. A non-person-centred approach might simply say “exercise more and eat less sugar.” A person-centred approach would consider his needs (managing blood glucose and weight), his wishes (he enjoys cooking and wants to stay independent), and his circumstances (limited mobility, lives alone, moderate income). The recommendation might include chair-based exercises, a referral to a dietitian who can suggest low-sugar recipes he can cook himself, and a local diabetes support group for social contact.

Importance for Individuals

When care is person-centred, individuals benefit in several important ways. These benefits are a common exam focus, so make sure you can explain each one with an example.

  • Comfort — individuals feel more comfortable with recommendations, advice and treatment because these have been designed around them, not imposed on them.
  • Confidence — they have greater confidence that the plan will work because it reflects their real situation.
  • Unique needs met — every person is different. Person-centred care ensures personal and cultural needs are respected.
  • Independence — by involving the individual in decisions, the approach promotes independence rather than dependence on professionals.
  • Motivation — individuals are more motivated to follow recommendations because they helped create them. They feel ownership of the plan.
  • Happiness — they feel happier and more positive about their health and wellbeing overall.
  • Support for vulnerable individuals — more vulnerable people receive increased, tailored support that addresses their specific risks.
Key Fact

Individuals who receive person-centred care are more likely to follow recommendations and take actions to improve their health, because the plan feels achievable and relevant to their life.

Benefits for Workers & Services

The person-centred approach does not only help the individual — it also benefits health and social care workers and the services they work for.

Job satisfaction — workers feel more fulfilled when they see individuals engaging with care plans and making real progress. Knowing that their work makes a genuine difference improves morale and reduces staff turnover.

Saves time — when recommendations are realistic and the individual is motivated, they are less likely to miss appointments or need repeated consultations for the same issue. This frees up time for other service users.

Saves money — fewer missed appointments and fewer repeat visits mean lower costs for the service. Prevention and early intervention also reduce the need for expensive emergency care later.

Reduces complaints — individuals who feel heard and respected are far less likely to complain. This protects the reputation of the service and reduces the time staff spend dealing with formal complaint procedures.

Linking Person-Centred Care to the 6 Cs

The person-centred approach is closely connected to the 6 Cs from Component 2. Care and compassion ensure the individual is treated with empathy and dignity. Communication means listening to the individual’s wishes. Competence ensures the professional has the knowledge to make appropriate recommendations. Courage means speaking up if a plan is not working. Commitment drives continuous improvement in the care experience.

Without person-centred care, individuals may feel that their views do not matter. This can lead to disengagement, missed appointments and worsening health outcomes. By contrast, when the approach is applied well, it creates a partnership between the professional and the individual that produces better results for everyone involved.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Component 3 exam, you will often be given a case study and asked to explain why a person-centred approach is important for that individual. Always refer to the individual’s specific needs, wishes and circumstances — generic answers that could apply to anyone will not reach the higher mark bands. Use the case study details to show how person-centred care leads to specific benefits such as increased motivation or greater independence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The person-centred approach considers the individual’s needs, wishes and circumstances to create tailored care plans.
  • It benefits individuals through increased comfort, confidence, independence and motivation to follow recommendations.
  • It benefits workers and services by improving job satisfaction, saving time and money, and reducing complaints.

lessons.title: Recommendations to Improve Health
lessons.description: Established health recommendations and the formal and informal support available to follow them.
lessons.content_html:
Why Recommendations Matter

Once a health professional has assessed an individual’s physiological and lifestyle indicators, the next step is to make recommendations — specific actions the person can take to improve their health and wellbeing. These recommendations must be person-centred, realistic and linked to the indicators that were identified as abnormal.

In the Component 3 exam, you will often be given a case study with physiological data and asked to suggest appropriate recommendations. This lesson covers the established recommendations and the support available to help people follow them.

Established Recommendations

The Pearson spec identifies eight key areas where recommendations can be made. Each one targets a different aspect of physical health.

Key Fact

The eight established recommendations are: improving resting heart rate and recovery rate after exercise, improving blood pressure, maintaining a healthy weight, eating a balanced diet, getting enough physical activity, quitting smoking, sensible alcohol consumption, and stopping substance misuse.

Recommendations in Detail

Improving resting heart rate and recovery rate — a resting heart rate above 100 bpm is considered high. Regular cardiovascular exercise (such as brisk walking, swimming or cycling) strengthens the heart muscle, lowering the resting rate over time. A faster recovery rate after exercise shows improved fitness.

Improving blood pressure — high blood pressure (140/90 mmHg or above) increases the risk of stroke and heart disease. Recommendations include reducing salt and saturated fat intake, taking regular exercise, managing stress and, if necessary, taking prescribed medication.

Maintaining a healthy weight — a BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m² is considered healthy. Overweight or obese individuals are advised to increase physical activity and reduce calorie intake. Underweight individuals may need to eat more nutrient-rich foods.

Eating a balanced diet — the Eatwell Guide recommends eating plenty of fruit, vegetables and starchy carbohydrates, moderate amounts of protein and dairy, and small amounts of unsaturated fats and oils. Sugary and high-fat foods should be limited.

Getting enough physical activity — the UK Chief Medical Officers recommend that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity. Children and young people should aim for 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.

Quitting smoking — smoking damages the lungs and cardiovascular system. Recommendations include using nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum or inhalers), prescription medications, and support from NHS Stop Smoking services.

Sensible alcohol consumption — the UK guidelines recommend no more than 14 units of alcohol per week, spread over three or more days, with several alcohol-free days each week. Binge drinking is particularly harmful.

Stopping substance misuse — misuse of substances such as cannabis, opiates (e.g. heroin) or other drugs has severe physical and mental health consequences. Recommendations focus on accessing professional treatment and support services.

In the exam, you must link each recommendation to the correct indicator. For example, if a person has a BMI of 31 kg/m² (obese), the recommendation is to maintain a healthy weight through diet and exercise. If their resting heart rate is 105 bpm, the recommendation is regular cardiovascular exercise to bring it down. Always use the specific data from the case study to justify your recommendation.

Formal Support

Formal support comes from trained professionals and organised services. It includes:

  • Professionals — GPs, nurses, dietitians, physiotherapists, counsellors and other qualified practitioners who provide expert advice, treatment and monitoring.
  • Trained volunteers — people who give their time and have received training to support others, for example at NHS Stop Smoking services or mental health helplines.
  • Support groups — organised groups where people with similar conditions meet to share experiences and encouragement, such as Alcoholics Anonymous, Weight Watchers or local diabetes groups.
  • Charities — organisations such as the British Heart Foundation, Mind or Macmillan Cancer Support that provide information, helplines, practical resources and sometimes financial assistance.
Key Fact

Formal support is provided by professionals, trained volunteers, support groups and charities. Informal support comes from friends, family, neighbours, community members and work colleagues.

Informal Support

Informal support comes from the people around the individual in their everyday life. It is not organised or professionally delivered, but it can be just as important.

  • Friends — can provide emotional encouragement, exercise with the individual, or help them stick to a healthier routine.
  • Family — can help with practical tasks such as cooking healthier meals, attending appointments together, or providing transport.
  • Neighbours — can check on the individual, offer lifts to appointments, or reduce feelings of isolation.
  • Community and work colleagues — workplace wellbeing programmes, community sports clubs or faith groups can all provide motivation and social support.

Rosa is 45 and wants to quit smoking. Her GP (formal support) prescribes nicotine patches and refers her to a local NHS Stop Smoking group (formal support). Her sister (informal support) agrees to be her “quit buddy” and texts her encouraging messages. Her colleague at work (informal support) stops offering her cigarette breaks and instead suggests short walks. This combination of formal and informal support gives Rosa the best chance of success.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When recommending improvements in the exam, always make your suggestions specific to the case study. Do not just write “eat a balanced diet” — explain what that means for the individual, for example “replace fast food lunches with home-prepared meals following the Eatwell Guide.” Then suggest both formal support (e.g. dietitian referral) and informal support (e.g. family helping with meal preparation) to show depth.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are eight established recommendations for improving health, ranging from improving heart rate to stopping substance misuse.
  • Formal support (professionals, volunteers, support groups, charities) and informal support (friends, family, neighbours, community) both play vital roles.
  • In the exam, always link recommendations to specific indicators and use both types of support in your answers.

lessons.title: Barriers & Obstacles to Health
lessons.description: System-level barriers vs personal obstacles and how each can be overcome.
lessons.content_html:
Why People Struggle to Follow Recommendations

Even when an individual receives excellent person-centred care and realistic recommendations, they may still find it difficult to follow through. The reasons fall into two distinct categories: barriers and obstacles. Understanding the difference between these two concepts is essential for the Component 3 exam.

Key Fact

Barriers are system-level problems — they exist within the health and social care system and prevent an individual from accessing a service. Obstacles are personal to the individual — they come from the person’s own life, emotions or circumstances and make it difficult for them to act on recommendations.

Barriers (System-Level)

Barriers are features of the health and social care system itself that stop people from getting the help they need. The spec identifies seven types of barrier.

Physical barriers — problems getting into and around healthcare facilities. For example, a wheelchair user may not be able to access a building without a ramp, or corridors may be too narrow. These can be overcome with ramps, wider doorways, accessible toilets, stair lifts and hoists.

Sensory disability barriers — difficulties faced by people with hearing or visual impairments. Information may not be available in accessible formats. Solutions include hearing loops, British Sign Language (BSL) interpreters, communication cards, large print and braille leaflets, and staff collecting vulnerable service users from waiting areas.

Social and cultural barriers — lack of awareness about services, differing cultural beliefs, social stigma (for example, around mental health), or fear of losing independence. These can be addressed through awareness campaigns, choice of service provider (such as a male or female practitioner), and collaboration with community and faith groups.

Language and speech barriers — faced by people who speak English as an additional language or who have speech impairments. Solutions include literature in other languages, face-to-face and telephone interpretation services, longer appointments, use of advocates, and staff training on common speech difficulties.

Geographical barriers — the distance to a service provider or poor transport links. People in rural areas are especially affected. Solutions include local community transport schemes, home and community visits, community clinics and telehealth schemes.

Resource barriers — where the service provider itself lacks the resources (staff, equipment, facilities) to meet demand. This might mean long waiting lists or limited appointment availability.

Financial barriers — some services involve charges, and there are also transport costs and potential loss of income while attending appointments. Support includes NHS exemption certificates, the NHS Low Income Scheme, NHS vouchers for eye tests, glasses and lenses, the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme (HTCS), and charitable community transport.

For each barrier, there are specific ways it can be overcome by the service provider or user. In the exam, you should name the barrier, explain how it affects the individual in the case study, and then suggest a realistic way to overcome it. For example: “Aisha faces a language barrier because she speaks Urdu as her first language. This could be overcome by the GP surgery providing a telephone interpretation service during her appointment.”

Obstacles (Personal/Individual-Level)

Obstacles come from within the individual or their personal circumstances. They are not caused by the system but by the person’s own situation. The spec identifies five types of obstacle.

Emotional and psychological obstacles — lack of motivation, low self-esteem, acceptance of their current state (“this is just how I am”), anxiety or stress. A person who is depressed may not feel able to start exercising even though they know it would help.

Time constraints — work and family commitments can make it very difficult to attend appointments, cook healthy meals, or find time for exercise. A single parent working two jobs has little spare time.

Availability of resources — the individual may lack the financial resources to buy healthy food, the equipment for exercise, or access to amenities like a gym or swimming pool.

Unachievable targets — if the recommendations set targets that are too ambitious or the timescale is unrealistic, the individual may give up. For example, telling someone to lose three stone in two months is not achievable for most people.

Lack of support — without encouragement from family and friends, it is much harder to make and sustain lifestyle changes. A person trying to quit smoking is more likely to relapse if everyone around them still smokes.

Key Fact

Obstacles also include other factors specific to the individual, such as ability or disability, existing health conditions, or addiction. These personal factors make it harder for the individual to follow recommendations even when services are accessible.

Scenario: Kwame is 40 and has been advised to attend a weight management programme at his local hospital. He lives 15 miles away and does not drive. He also feels embarrassed about his weight and lacks motivation.

Barrier (system-level): The geographical distance and poor transport links are a barrier. This is not Kwame’s fault — it is a problem with the location and accessibility of the service. It could be overcome by offering a community-based programme closer to his home or a telehealth alternative.

Obstacle (personal): Kwame’s embarrassment and lack of motivation are personal obstacles. They come from his emotions, not from the system. These could be addressed through emotional support from friends or family, counselling, or a supportive group environment.

Overcoming Barriers & Obstacles Together

In practice, individuals often face both barriers and obstacles at the same time. A strong exam answer will identify both types, explain how they affect the individual in the case study, and suggest person-centred ways to overcome them using formal and informal support.

Advocates can help overcome language barriers by speaking on behalf of the individual. Support groups can address emotional obstacles by providing peer encouragement. The key is matching the right solution to the right problem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The examiner will test whether you understand the difference between barriers and obstacles. A common mistake is to confuse them. Remember: a barrier is part of the system (e.g. no wheelchair ramp, no interpreter available, clinic too far away). An obstacle is personal to the individual (e.g. low motivation, lack of family support, time pressures). If you label them correctly and justify your choice, you will access the higher mark bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Barriers are system-level problems (physical access, sensory, social/cultural, language, geographical, resource, financial) that prevent individuals from accessing services.
  • Obstacles are personal to the individual (emotional/psychological, time constraints, resource availability, unachievable targets, lack of support) and make action difficult.
  • In the exam, correctly identify and distinguish barriers from obstacles, then suggest person-centred ways to overcome each one.
