lessons.title: Human Lifespan Development
lessons.description: The six life stages and how PIES development changes from infancy to later adulthood.
lessons.content_html:
Why Lifespan Development Matters for Component 3

Component 3 is a synoptic exam, which means it draws on knowledge from Components 1 and 2 as well as the Component 3 content itself. One of the most important areas you need to revise is human lifespan development from Component 1. In the exam, you may need to explain how an individual’s life stage affects their health needs, their ability to follow recommendations, or the type of support they require.

The Six Life Stages

The Pearson specification divides human life into six stages. Each stage has distinct characteristics across the four PIES categories: Physical, Intellectual, Emotional and Social development.

Key Fact

The six life stages are: infancy (birth to 2 years), early childhood (3–8 years), adolescence (9–18 years), early adulthood (19–45 years), middle adulthood (46–65 years) and later adulthood (65+ years).

Infancy (Birth to 2 Years)

Physical: Rapid growth in weight and height. Development of gross motor skills (sitting, crawling, walking) and fine motor skills (grasping, holding). Infants follow the same pattern of development but at different rates.

Intellectual: Rapid development of language skills (babbling, first words) and thinking skills such as memory and recall.

Emotional: Attachments are formed with primary carers. Emotional wellbeing is based on bonding, attachment, security and contentment.

Social: Strong dependence on adults and carers. Socialisation happens through the family. Infants engage in solitary play.

Early Childhood (3–8 Years)

Physical: Continued growth. Mastery of gross and fine motor skills (running, writing, using scissors).

Intellectual: Increased curiosity about the world. Language fluency develops. Strong grasp of memory and recall.

Emotional: Increased independence. Wider range of relationships formed. Emotional wellbeing still based on attachment, security and contentment.

Social: Social circle widens. Close friendships are formed. Socialisation continues through family and also friends and carers. Social play develops (playing with others rather than alone).

Adolescence (9–18 Years)

Physical: Onset of puberty with primary and secondary sexual characteristics developing. Physical differences between males and females become more pronounced.

Intellectual: Complex and abstract thinking develops, allowing adolescents to consider hypothetical situations and reason logically.

Emotional: Greater independence and more freedom to make decisions. Concerns over self-image and self-esteem may increase. Emotional wellbeing remains based on attachment, security and contentment.

Social: Wide range of formal and informal relationships develop and have influence. Peer pressure becomes important. Intimate relationships may form.

Early Adulthood (19–45 Years)

Physical: Peak physical fitness is reached. Full height attained. Sexual maturity reached; women are at their most fertile.

Intellectual: Mastery of abstract and creative thinking. Careers become important. Some individuals may return to education.

Emotional: Independent living and control over own life. Emotional wellbeing based on attachment, security and contentment.

Social: Intimate and long-lasting relationships are formed, including marriage, civil partnerships and parenthood.

Physical: By the end of this stage, the ageing process begins. Women experience the menopause.

Intellectual: Can use accumulated knowledge and experience for complex decision making. Some may retire towards the end of this stage.

Emotional: May experience changes in self-image and self-esteem linked to retirement or the ageing process. Emotional wellbeing based on attachment, security and contentment.

Social: May have more time to socialise as children grow up and leave home. Social networks may shift.

Physical: The ageing process continues. Decline in strength and fitness. Loss of mobility. Loss of muscle tone and skin elasticity.

Intellectual: May experience decline in cognitive ability, such as loss of memory and recall. Risk of conditions like dementia.

Emotional: May become more dependent on others, which can affect self-esteem. Emotional wellbeing remains based on attachment, security and contentment.

Social: May experience bereavement and a reduction in social circle. Risk of social isolation and loneliness.

Key Patterns Across the Life Stages

Notice that emotional wellbeing at every stage is based on attachment, security and contentment. This is a recurring theme throughout the spec. Physical development follows a pattern of growth and peak in early adulthood, followed by gradual decline from middle adulthood onwards. Intellectual development progresses from simple to complex thinking, and social development moves from dependence on family towards wider relationships and then, in some cases, back towards a smaller social circle in later life. Understanding these patterns helps you predict how an individual’s life stage will affect their health needs.

Factors Affecting Growth & Development

Growth and development across the life stages can be affected by a range of factors. These mirror the factors you studied in Component 3’s Area A, but here the focus is on long-term developmental impact rather than current health status.

  • Physical factors — inherited conditions (sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy), illness, mental ill health, physical ill health, disabilities, sensory impairments.
  • Lifestyle factors — nutrition, physical activity, smoking, substance misuse.
  • Emotional factors — fear, anxiety, grief, happiness, security, attachment.
  • Social factors — supportive and unsupportive relationships, social inclusion/exclusion, bullying, discrimination.
  • Cultural factors — religion, gender roles, gender identity, sexual orientation, community participation.
  • Environmental factors — housing conditions, home environment, exposure to pollution.
  • Economic factors — employment situation, financial resources.
Key Fact

Factors can affect development positively or negatively, and different factors impact different PIES areas. For example, bullying (a social factor) can negatively affect emotional development (low self-esteem) and social development (withdrawal from friendships).
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Component 3 exam, case studies will often specify the individual’s age. Use this to identify their life stage and then explain how the typical PIES characteristics of that stage affect their health needs and their ability to follow recommendations. For example, a person in later adulthood may have declining physical fitness, making vigorous exercise unrealistic — so chair-based exercises would be more appropriate.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are six life stages, each with distinct PIES characteristics: infancy, early childhood, adolescence, early adulthood, middle adulthood and later adulthood.
  • Seven categories of factors (physical, lifestyle, emotional, social, cultural, environmental, economic) can affect growth and development positively or negatively.
  • In the synoptic exam, link the individual’s life stage and PIES development to the recommendations and support they need.

lessons.title: Life Events & Coping with Change
lessons.description: Types of life events, character traits that influence coping, and support available.
lessons.content_html:
Life Events in the Synoptic Exam

Component 3 is synoptic, which means the exam will test your ability to apply knowledge from Components 1 and 2 to health and wellbeing scenarios. A key area from Component 1 is understanding how life events affect individuals and how they cope with the changes these events bring. In the exam, you may be given a case study where an individual has experienced a life event and asked to explain its impact on their health and wellbeing, or to suggest how they could be supported.

Types of Life Event

The Pearson specification groups life events into three categories. Each type can affect an individual’s PIES development in different ways.

Key Fact

The three types of life event are: health and wellbeing events (accident/injury, physical illness, mental and emotional health issues), relationship changes (entering relationships, marriage, divorce, parenthood, bereavement) and life circumstances (moving house/school/job, exclusion from education, redundancy, imprisonment, changes to standards of living, retirement).

Health & Wellbeing Events

These are events that directly affect an individual’s physical or mental health. They include:

  • Accident or injury — can cause sudden physical changes (loss of mobility, pain), emotional distress (anxiety, fear of recurrence) and social changes (unable to work or socialise).
  • Physical illness — a diagnosis such as cancer or diabetes can affect all four PIES areas, causing physical limitations, worry and stress, changes in self-image, and withdrawal from social activities.
  • Mental and emotional health — conditions such as depression or anxiety can reduce motivation, affect concentration (intellectual), lower self-esteem (emotional) and lead to social isolation.

Relationship Changes

Changes in relationships can have both positive and negative effects on an individual’s development:

  • Entering relationships, marriage or civil partnership — often positive, providing emotional security, companionship and a wider social network.
  • Divorce or separation — can cause grief, loss of financial security, changes to living arrangements and emotional distress.
  • Parenthood — brings joy and purpose but also stress, sleep deprivation and changes to social life and finances.
  • Bereavement — the death of a loved one can cause intense grief, affecting emotional wellbeing, physical health (not eating, not sleeping) and social withdrawal.

Life Circumstances

Changes in life circumstances can be planned or unplanned, and they disrupt an individual’s routine and sense of stability:

  • Moving house, school or job — involves adapting to new environments, forming new relationships and potentially losing existing support networks.
  • Exclusion from education — can damage self-esteem, limit intellectual development and reduce social contact.
  • Redundancy — loss of income, purpose and daily routine. Can lead to financial stress and emotional difficulties.
  • Imprisonment — loss of freedom and social contact. Can affect mental health and relationships with family.
  • Changes to standards of living — moving into poverty or gaining wealth both require adjustment and affect physical and emotional wellbeing.
  • Retirement — can bring freedom and leisure time but also loss of identity, reduced income and risk of social isolation.

Character Traits That Influence Coping

People react very differently to the same type of event. The spec identifies four character traits that influence how well an individual copes with change.

Resilience — the ability to bounce back from setbacks. A resilient person can face a life event and recover more quickly, adapting to the new situation.

Self-esteem — how a person feels about themselves. High self-esteem gives confidence to seek help and believe they can cope. Low self-esteem makes it harder to take positive action.

Emotional intelligence — the ability to recognise, understand and manage one’s own emotions and the emotions of others. People with high emotional intelligence can process difficult feelings constructively rather than being overwhelmed.

Disposition — a person’s overall character traits, such as being naturally positive, optimistic or negative. A positive disposition helps a person see opportunities in change, while a negative disposition may lead to focusing on the worst outcomes.

Key Fact

Two people can experience the same life event but cope very differently depending on their resilience, self-esteem, emotional intelligence and disposition. The exam often asks you to explain why this happens.

Sources of Support

When individuals face life events, various sources of support can help them adapt. The spec identifies five key sources:

  • Family, friends, neighbours, partners — provide emotional comfort, practical help and companionship.
  • Professional carers and services — GPs, counsellors, social workers and other trained professionals who provide expert guidance.
  • Community groups, voluntary and faith-based organisations — provide a sense of belonging, practical assistance and shared understanding.
  • Multi-agency working — different services working together, e.g. social services working with a mental health trust, or children’s services working with the justice system.
  • Multidisciplinary working — professionals from different disciplines working together, e.g. a health visitor working with a GP, or a psychiatric nurse with an occupational therapist.

Types of Support

The support provided can take different forms, depending on what the individual needs:

  • Emotional support — listening, comfort, reassurance and encouragement to help the person process their feelings.
  • Information and advice — providing relevant facts, guidance, signposting to services, and endorsed apps that help the individual understand their situation and options.
  • Practical help — financial assistance (benefits, grants), support with childcare, help with domestic chores, transport to appointments.

Carol, aged 58, has recently lost her husband after a long illness. Her character traits: she has moderate resilience but low self-esteem. Her disposition is generally negative — she tends to focus on problems rather than solutions.

Sources of support: Her daughter visits weekly (family). Her GP has referred her to a bereavement counsellor (professional service). She attends a local church group (faith-based organisation).

Types of support: The counsellor provides emotional support by helping her process grief. The church group provides practical help with transport to appointments and social contact. Her GP provides information and advice about coping strategies and local support groups.

Carol’s low self-esteem means she may not believe she can cope alone, so professional emotional support is particularly important. Her negative disposition means she may need encouragement to see progress, which her daughter and church group can provide.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering synoptic questions about life events, structure your response around three parts: (1) identify the life event and its type, (2) explain its impact on the individual’s PIES development, and (3) suggest appropriate sources and types of support. Always link the character traits to how well the individual copes — this is where the synoptic marks are.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Life events fall into three categories: health and wellbeing events, relationship changes and life circumstances, each affecting PIES development.
  • Four character traits (resilience, self-esteem, emotional intelligence, disposition) influence how well an individual copes with change.
  • Support comes from various sources (family, professionals, community groups, multi-agency/multidisciplinary working) and takes three forms: emotional, informational and practical.

lessons.title: Care Values, Services & Skills
lessons.description: The 6 Cs of care, essential skills and attributes, and how barriers to services can be overcome.
lessons.content_html:
Why Care Values Matter in Component 3

Component 3 is a synoptic exam that draws on knowledge from all three components. One of the most important areas from Component 2 is the values, skills and attributes required to give care. In the exam, you may be asked to explain how a care professional should demonstrate these when supporting an individual, or how they help overcome obstacles. This lesson revises the key content you need.

The 6 Cs

The 6 Cs were developed to ensure consistent, high-quality care across all health and social care settings. Every professional is expected to demonstrate these values in their daily practice.

Key Fact

The 6 Cs are: Care (receiving correct and consistent care), Compassion (empathy, respect and dignity), Competence (skills and knowledge to deliver effective care based on research), Communication (involving individuals and/or carers and listening), Courage (doing the right thing and speaking up when concerns arise), and Commitment (to improving care and experience for individuals).

The 6 Cs in Detail

Care — every individual deserves correct and consistent care that meets their needs. This means providing the right treatment, at the right time, every time. It is the foundation that all other values are built upon.

Compassion — treating individuals with empathy, respect and dignity. Compassionate care means seeing the person behind the condition and understanding how they feel. It involves listening without judgement and responding kindly.

Competence — having the skills, knowledge and expertise to deliver effective care. Competent professionals keep their knowledge up to date through research and training. They follow evidence-based practice to ensure the best outcomes.

Communication — involving individuals and their carers in decisions about their care and truly listening to their views. Good communication builds trust, ensures the person feels heard, and reduces misunderstandings. It includes verbal, non-verbal and written communication.

Courage — doing the right thing, even when it is difficult. This means speaking up when there are concerns about safety, quality of care or the behaviour of colleagues. It also means being honest with individuals about their condition and prognosis.

Commitment — a dedication to improving care and the experience of individuals. Committed professionals continuously reflect on their practice, seek feedback and strive to do better.

A nurse is caring for Mr Patel, aged 78, who has dementia and lives in a care home. Care: The nurse ensures Mr Patel receives his medication at the correct time. Compassion: She speaks gently and at his pace, showing respect for his dignity. Competence: She has completed dementia awareness training. Communication: She involves his daughter in care decisions and listens to Mr Patel’s preferences. Courage: She reports a colleague who raised their voice at Mr Patel. Commitment: She attends regular training sessions to improve her dementia care skills.

Skills in Health & Social Care

The spec identifies four key skills that health and social care professionals need:

  • Problem solving — the ability to identify issues and find workable solutions. For example, a social worker finding alternative accommodation for a vulnerable adult whose home is unsafe.
  • Observation — noticing changes in an individual’s behaviour, appearance or condition that may indicate a change in their health or wellbeing. Early observation can prevent problems from escalating.
  • Dealing with difficult situations — remaining calm and professional when facing challenging scenarios such as conflicts, complaints, aggressive behaviour or emergencies.
  • Organisation — managing time, resources, appointments and records efficiently. Good organisation ensures that nothing is missed and care is consistent.

Attributes in Health & Social Care

Attributes are personal qualities that professionals need alongside their skills. The spec identifies four:

  • Empathy — the ability to understand and share the feelings of another person. Different from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone. Empathy means putting yourself in their shoes.
  • Patience — the ability to stay calm and give individuals the time they need, whether it’s a child learning to talk or an older adult struggling to dress themselves.
  • Trustworthiness — being reliable, keeping promises and maintaining confidentiality. Individuals must be able to trust their care providers with sensitive information.
  • Honesty — being truthful with individuals about their condition, treatment options and prognosis. Honesty builds trust and enables informed decision-making.
Key Fact

Skills are practical abilities (what a professional does), while attributes are personal qualities (what a professional is like). Both are essential for delivering high-quality, person-centred care.

Barriers to Accessing Services & How to Overcome Them

From Component 2, you also need to remember the barriers that prevent individuals from accessing health and social care services and how these can be overcome. This links directly to Component 3’s barriers and obstacles content (Lesson 9).

Physical barriers (e.g. no wheelchair access) → overcome by ramps, wider doorways, accessible toilets, stair lifts, hoists.

Sensory barriers (e.g. hearing or visual impairments) → overcome by hearing loops, BSL interpreters, large print, braille, communication cards.

Social and cultural barriers (e.g. stigma, cultural beliefs) → overcome by awareness campaigns, choice of practitioner, collaboration with faith groups.

Language barriers (e.g. EAL speakers, speech impairments) → overcome by interpretation services, literature in other languages, longer appointments, advocates.

Geographical barriers (e.g. remote location) → overcome by community transport, home visits, telehealth.

Financial barriers (e.g. cost of services or transport) → overcome by NHS exemptions, Low Income Scheme, Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme.

Learning disability barriers → overcome by Health Passports, advocates, Learning Disability Nurses, “Quiet Clinics,” easy-read leaflets, the Accessible Information Standard.

Benefits of Skills, Attributes & Values in Practice

When professionals demonstrate the correct skills, attributes and values, individuals benefit in many ways. They are supported to overcome personal obstacles, receive high-quality and person-centred care, are treated with respect, are empowered and have their independence maintained, are protected from harm, feel comfortable raising complaints, and have their dignity, privacy, confidentiality and rights protected.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam asks how skills, attributes or values benefit an individual, do not simply list the 6 Cs. Instead, pick the most relevant ones for the case study and explain how each one would improve the individual’s experience in that specific situation. For example: “Communication is important for Maya because she speaks English as an additional language. The nurse demonstrating good communication would use simple language, check Maya understands, and arrange an interpreter if needed.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 6 Cs (Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage, Commitment) are the core values that underpin all health and social care practice.
  • Skills (problem solving, observation, dealing with difficult situations, organisation) and attributes (empathy, patience, trustworthiness, honesty) are both needed for high-quality care.
  • Barriers to accessing services can be physical, sensory, social/cultural, language, geographical, financial or related to learning disability — each has specific ways to overcome it.

practice_questions.marks: Indicative content: Sensory barrier — hospital staff may not know BSL, written information may be the only format available (1). Ways to overcome: BSL interpreter provided at appointments (1), communication cards (1), staff collecting Zara from waiting area (visual announcements may not be available) (1), hearing loop if she has partial hearing (1). Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation covering benefits of courage (protects vulnerable individuals, maintains standards, prevents harm, builds trust) and challenges (fear of repercussions, conflict with colleagues, emotional difficulty). practice_questions.text: Hassan is 82 and has dementia. He lives in a care home. His family are concerned that he is not being treated with dignity and that staff do not always communicate effectively with him. Using your knowledge of the 6 Cs, skills and attributes, explain how care staff should be supporting Hassan. Discuss how demonstrating these values would benefit Hassan.
practice_questions.marks: Lower band (1-3): Superficial identification of values with little link to Hassan. Lower-mid band (4-5): Some values/skills identified but not applied to Hassan's specific situation. Upper-mid band (6-8): Clear application of relevant 6 Cs: Care (consistent, correct medication and routines), Compassion (treating Hassan with dignity, speaking at his level), Communication (using simple language, involving family in decisions, patience in listening), Competence (dementia training). Skills: observation (noticing changes in Hassan's condition), patience (giving him time). Benefits: dignity maintained, family reassured, quality of life improved, Hassan feels safe and respected. Top band (9-10): Comprehensive response applying all relevant 6 Cs, skills and attributes to Hassan's specific situation. Explains how each value benefits him personally (e.g. communication reduces his confusion and anxiety, courage means staff report concerns about poor practice). Makes connections between values (e.g. competence supports communication because trained staff know how to interact with dementia patients). Considers benefits for both Hassan and the care home (fewer complaints, better staff morale).

glossary_terms.definition: Six core values that underpin all health and social care practice: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage and Commitment.
The ability to manage challenging scenarios in care settings calmly and professionally, including conflicts, complaints or emergency situations.
Personal qualities that health and social care workers should possess, which help build trust and provide high-quality care.
Something personal to an individual that blocks them from moving forward or when action is prevented or made difficult.
